nameStory: The 'lovegrass' name comes from the delicate, airy appearance of this grass's seed heads that seem to float like wisps of affection in the breeze. The 'little' part distinguishes it from its taller cousins in the lovegrass family. It's also called 'smaller stinkgrass' because when crushed, the leaves can give off a slightly unpleasant odor.
description: Little Lovegrass is a small, delicate annual grass that forms loose tufts or clumps. It typically grows 6-18 inches tall with fine, thread-like leaves and airy, open seed heads that give it a feathery appearance. This introduced grass from the Old World has adapted well to disturbed areas throughout New England, though it's not commonly encountered here. Despite being a grass, it produces tiny flowers arranged in loose, branching clusters that catch the light beautifully.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers arranged in loose, open, branching clusters that look almost cloud-like; each individual spikelet is so small you'll need to look closely, but the overall effect is delicate and airy

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, thread-like leaves that feel smooth between your fingers; they're typically blue-green to gray-green and may smell slightly unpleasant when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small tufts or clumps, usually 6-18 inches tall, with multiple stems arising from the base; has an overall delicate, wispy appearance

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces extremely tiny seeds in late summer that are technically edible but so small they're barely worth collecting; they'll feel like fine grains of sand

habitat: Look for Little Lovegrass in disturbed, sandy or gravelly areas with little competition from other plants. It thrives along railroad tracks, roadsides, sidewalk cracks, vacant lots, and other waste areas where the soil is poor and compacted. In New England, it's quite rare, preferring the warmest, most disturbed sites.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small tufts of narrow leaves, easily overlooked among other grasses and weeds in disturbed areas.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive airy flower heads develop and become most noticeable, creating the plant's characteristic delicate, cloud-like appearance.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the plant begins to turn brown and dry out, with the seed heads becoming even more wispy and catching in the wind.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving only seeds to germinate the following spring.

funFact: This humble little grass produces seeds so tiny that they were historically used as emergency famine food, but you'd need to collect thousands of plants just to make a small handful of grain - each seed is smaller than a pinhead!
confusionNotes: Little Lovegrass can be confused with other small, delicate grasses, but its extremely fine, thread-like leaves and distinctively airy, open seed heads help set it apart. Remember: if it looks like a miniature cloud on a stick, it's probably a lovegrass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its romantic name, Little Lovegrass is considered a weedy species that's native to Africa and Asia but has spread worldwide. In New England, it's at the northern edge of its range and remains quite uncommon, making any sighting noteworthy.
compareHints: Among the lovegrasses in New England, Little Lovegrass is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking. Purple Lovegrass tends to be taller with more colorful seed heads, while other lovegrasses in our region are generally more robust. Little Lovegrass's extremely fine texture and preference for the most disturbed sites help distinguish it from its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple Lovegrass is the showiest of New England's lovegrasses, with much larger and more colorful flower clusters than its relatives like Little Lovegrass or Teal Lovegrass.
Among New England's lovegrasses, purple lovegrass is distinguished by its compact, tufted growth habit and relatively small size.

Teal lovegrass stands out from its lovegrass relatives primarily by its wetland habitat - while purple lovegrass, little lovegrass, and most others prefer dry, disturbed soils, teal lovegrass is the water-lover of the family.
African lovegrass differs from other New England lovegrasses by its distinctive weeping growth habit and blue-gray foliage color.
Among New England's love-grasses, Jersey Love-grass is the most delicate and airy-looking.
Tiny lovegrass lives up to its name by being much smaller and more delicate than its lovegrass relatives like purple lovegrass, which forms more substantial clumps.

Among the lovegrasses, Frank's Lovegrass sits in the middle size-wise—larger than Tiny Lovegrass with its hair-thin appearance, but smaller and less showy than Purple Lovegrass which often forms more substantial clumps.
